clinical_record:
A 70-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distension. Pelvic ultrasound revealed an 18-cm solid–cystic mass occupying the pelvic and abdominal cavities with rich intralesional blood flow. Laboratory studies showed a serum CA-125 level of 367.9 U/mL, neuron-specific enolase of 24.83 ng/mL, and CYFRA21-1 of 3.85 ng/mL. At laparotomy, 0.5 L of hemorrhagic ascites was evacuated. Examination revealed a 20-cm right ovarian cystic and solid mass infiltrating the uterus, intestinal loops, and parietal pelvic wall, with diffuse peritoneal implants on the surface of the uterus and intestines; the left ovary, fallopian tube, and pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes appeared normal. A right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed and frozen section analysis demonstrated a poorly differentiated carcinoma. Consequently, a total abdominal hysterectomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, and resection of visible pelvic metastases was carried out. Grossly, the right ovarian tumor measured 33 × 23 × 5 cm, had a fragile nodular “rotten-flesh” surface, and its cut surface showed gray-white solid areas with hemorrhage and necrosis. The largest pelvic metastasis measured 12 × 10 × 3.5 cm, had an irregular dusty-pink external surface, and showed cystic and hemorrhagic regions on sectioning. Histologic examination of H&E-stained sections revealed predominantly trabecular and rosette-like formations of pleomorphic hyperchromatic tumor cells with moderate cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei (occasionally with conspicuous nucleoli and coarse chromatin), and a high mitotic rate.

MR is a male neonate born at 38 weeks’ gestation by elective cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 2350 g (5th–10th percentile), length 45 cm (5th percentile), head circumference 31 cm (<5th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes.  
Maternal history was notable only for immunity to rubella, negative toxoplasma serology, and a single CMV serology at 11 weeks (IgG positive, IgM negative). A maternal febrile episode occurred in the periconceptional period; there was no trauma, and no use of cocaine, warfarin, or anticonvulsants. No family history of bleeding disorders or stroke.  
Fetal ultrasound at 20 weeks suggested intracranial hemorrhage, confirmed by fetal MRI at 25 weeks, which showed a 2.3 cm porencephalic cyst in the right frontotemporal–insular region with ex vacuo enlargement of the right lateral ventricle, reduced right cerebral hemisphere volume, and abnormal micropolygyria of the right frontal cortex.  
At birth, examination revealed microcephaly, jaundice, micropurpura on the face and upper thorax, mild upper limb hypertonicity, and abnormal deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, assays of clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XIII), protein C and S, von Willebrand factor, alpha-2 antiplasmin, antithrombin, APC resistance, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies, were all normal. Gene sequencing for MTHFR and factor V Leiden was wild type. Newborn metabolic screening was negative.  
Cranial ultrasound on day 1 showed a right porencephalic area with “ex vacuo” enlargement of the right lateral ventricle and a germinolytic cyst on the left; MRI confirmed these findings, with no vascular malformations or thrombosis.

A 20-year-old unmarried girl, deaf and mute since birth, presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging left vulvar swelling that had become extremely painful during the past week. She had no fever or vaginal discharge. On examination, her vital signs were stable and she was afebrile, with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Local examination showed a left labial swelling with signs of inflammation, and a clinical diagnosis of Bartholin’s abscess was made; she was started on parenteral antibiotics. Within 24 hours, her pain decreased and the inflammation subsided. Because the patient and her parents insisted that she was sexually naïve, the lesion was reexamined. Now noted was a 5 × 5 cm swelling of the left labia majora without signs of inflammation; the mass was firm (not cystic), the labia minora were not everted, and the hymen was intact.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a painless lump in the left cheek, first noted nine months earlier. She reported no toothache, numbness, or systemic symptoms and had no significant medical history. On examination, there was left facial asymmetry without skin changes. Palpation revealed a firm, mobile, non-tender mass approximately 4 cm in diameter, located deep in the left buccal space and extending below the zygomatic arch; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraorally, there was a bulge of the left buccal mucosa; palpation confirmed a well-defined, firm, non-tender mass.

An orthopantomogram showed no bony destruction of the mandible or maxilla, with only a healed post-extraction socket in the region of tooth 36. Ultrasonography of the left cheek demonstrated a discrete, well-demarcated, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 2.6 × 2.0 cm, overlying the parotid gland, with no increase in internal vascular flow or calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed a well-bordered, slightly enhancing soft-tissue tumor measuring 2.7 × 3.7 × 4.0 cm in the left buccal space, indenting but not destroying adjacent bones (including the posterior maxillary sinus wall, medial pterygoid, masseter, and temporal muscle), and extending into the temporal space; the mass was supplied by branches of the left buccal artery.

Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded a hypocellular sample with erythrocytes, histiocytes, and neutrophils but showed “no signs of malignancy.” An intraoral incisional biopsy demonstrated “wide fibroblast proliferation, extremely similar to a fibroma.”
